title: The boy born on a Tuesday
objectives: Work out why a detail that sounds irrelevant moves the probability.
Count the 27 families with a Tuesday boy and find $\tfrac{13}{27}$.
See the answer move from $\tfrac{1}{3}$ towards $\tfrac{1}{2}$ as the detail gets rarer.

screens.title: The boy born on a Tuesday
screens.prose: Last lesson, “at least one is a boy” gave two boys a chance of $\tfrac{1}{3}$. Now the fact comes with an extra detail that sounds irrelevant. We will test whether it is.

state.caption: 16 equally likely families, elder child first

screens.question: Compared with $\tfrac{1}{3}$, is the chance of two boys now higher, lower or the same?

options.why: You treated the time of birth as irrelevant. It changes which families fit, and not evenly.
You expected the extra detail to rule out two-boy families. A two-boy family has two chances to contain a morning boy.

hints.text: Which kind of family has two chances to contain a morning boy?
A two-boy family fits if either boy was born in the morning.
A mixed family has only one boy to check, a two-boy family has two. So the detail favours two-boy families.

feedback.correct: Two-boy families fit the news more easily.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare how easily each kind of family fits the news.

explain.text: A two-boy family fits the news if either boy was born in the morning. A mixed family fits only if its one boy was. So the detail favours two-boy families and pushes the chance above $\tfrac{1}{3}$; next we count.

options.text: A two-boy family has two chances to contain a Tuesday boy, so it fits the news almost twice as often
Nowhere: the day is independent, so the answer is $\tfrac{1}{3}$
options.why: You treated an independent detail as irrelevant news. The news is about the family, and two-boy families fit it more easily.

options.text: The detail names one child, so the answer is exactly $\tfrac{1}{2}$

options.why: You looked for something special about Tuesday. Every day gives $\tfrac{13}{27}$; what matters is how rare the detail is.

hints.text: How likely is a two-boy family to contain a Tuesday boy? A mixed family?
Two boys: $1 - (\tfrac{6}{7})^2 = \tfrac{13}{49}$. One boy: $\tfrac{7}{49}$.
Prior odds of two boys to mixed are $1 : 2$. Multiply by the likelihood ratio $\tfrac{13}{7}$ to get $13 : 14$.

feedback.correct: Independence holds, but the news is about the family.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare how often each kind of family fits the news.

byKey.irrelevant: You took “independent” to mean “irrelevant”. The detail is independent of the sibling, but two-boy families fit the news almost twice as often.

explain.text: A two-boy family contains a Tuesday boy with chance $\tfrac{13}{49}$, a mixed family with chance $\tfrac{7}{49}$. Prior odds of $1:2$ times a likelihood ratio of $\tfrac{13}{7}$ give $13:14$, so $\tfrac{13}{27}$. The day is independent of the sibling, but not of how the family fits the news.

screens.title: Rarer and rarer details
screens.prose: Let the detail take $k$ equally likely values: $k = 2$ for morning or afternoon, $k = 7$ for the day. The same count gives $\dfrac{2k - 1}{4k - 1}$. Move the slider to larger $k$.
screens.question: What value does the chance approach as the detail gets rarer?

options.why: That is $k = 1$, a detail every boy has. Rarer details push the chance up, not back.
That is $k = 7$. Move further: the curve keeps rising.
You expected the curve to keep climbing. It levels off below the dashed line at $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

hints.text: Read the caption at $k = 60$.
For large $k$, the $-1$ terms hardly matter.
$\dfrac{2k-1}{4k-1}$ is close to $\dfrac{2k}{4k} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ when $k$ is large.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move the slider to the far right and read the caption.

explain.text: As $k$ grows, $\tfrac{2k-1}{4k-1}$ approaches $\tfrac{2k}{4k} = \tfrac{1}{2}$. A birth time to the second picks out one child, just like “the elder is a boy”. At $k = 1$ the detail says nothing new and the answer is $\tfrac{1}{3}$.

screens.prose: Now derive the curve. A child is one of $2k$ equally likely types: $k$ kinds of boy and $k$ of girl. Families are the $(2k)^2$ cells of a $2k$ by $2k$ grid.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: Families that fit: the special boy's row and column, $2k + 2k$ cells, less the shared one: $4k - 1$
Two-boy families among those $4k - 1$: $k$ in the row plus $k$ in the column, less the shared one: $2k - 1$
Every cell is equally likely, so $P(\text{two boys} \mid \text{news}) = \dfrac{2k - 1}{4k - 1}$

hints.text: Count the families that fit before the two-boy families among them.
The ratio needs both counts.
Count the cross, then the two-boy cells in it, then divide, then check.

feedback.correct: Count the cross, count inside it, divide, then check.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. You need the size of the cross before you count inside it.

explain.text: Your Tuesday grid was the case $k = 7$: 27 in the cross and 13 two-boy cells. The $-1$ in each count is the shared cell, two special boys. As $k$ grows, that one cell matters less and the ratio tends to $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

screens.prose: A desk made two trades yesterday. Each made money with chance 0.6, independently, at a random minute of the 390-minute session. A compliance check asks one question: “Did at least one trade placed at 10:17 make money?” The answer is yes.

rows: At least one made money at 10:17

screens.question: Roughly what is the chance both trades made money?

options.why: You ignored the minute. The check named 10:17 in advance, so a yes almost singles out one trade.
You carried over $\tfrac{1}{2}$ from the boys. Here naming one trade leaves 0.6 for the other.
That is the chance before the check. A yes rules out loss-loss and more.

hints.text: How likely is it that both trades won at 10:17?
A rare detail nearly picks out one trade, like “the first trade made money”.
Once one trade is singled out as a winner, the other wins with chance 0.6.

feedback.correct: The timestamp nearly singles out one trade.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how close a one-minute detail comes to naming a particular trade.

explain.text: A yes about one named minute almost picks out one trade, so it acts like “this trade made money”. The exact answer is $\tfrac{779}{1299} \approx 0.5997$, against $\tfrac{3}{7} \approx 0.43$ without the minute. A report that just named a winner's minute would tell you only that a trade won, and the answer would stay at $\tfrac{3}{7}$.

ideas: “At least one is a boy born on a Tuesday” fits 27 of 196 families. Of those, 13 have two boys: $\tfrac{13}{27} \approx 0.481$.
A two-boy family has two chances to fit the news, a mixed family one, so the detail favours two boys.
The rarer the detail, the closer it comes to naming one child, and the closer the answer gets to $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

formula.name: A detail with k equally likely values
formula.tex: P(\text{two boys} \mid \text{a boy with the detail}) = \dfrac{2k - 1}{4k - 1}
formula.note: $k = 1$ gives $\tfrac{1}{3}$, $k = 7$ gives $\tfrac{13}{27}$, and large $k$ tends to $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

summary.trap: “The day is independent, so it cannot matter” confuses independence of the children with irrelevance of the news. The news is about the family.

explain.text: With 12 months, $k = 12$. The cross holds $4k - 1 = 47$ families and $2k - 1 = 23$ of them have two boys. So the chance is $\tfrac{23}{47} \approx 0.489$.
